questions.body: What is CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing)?
questions.keyPoints: A browser security mechanism that uses HTTP headers to tell browsers whether a cross-origin web app can access resources.

options.text: A browser security mechanism that uses HTTP response headers (like `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`) to dictate whether client scripts on one origin can read resources from another origin.
options.explanation: The Same-Origin Policy blocks client scripts from reading cross-origin HTTP responses by default. CORS headers allow servers to explicitly specify which origins are permitted to access their responses.

options.text: A firewall protocol that blocks DDoS attacks on routers.
options.explanation: CORS is enforced client-side by browsers, not network firewalls.

options.text: A database synchronization protocol between SQL databases.
options.explanation: CORS is purely an HTTP browser security mechanism.

options.text: A client-side encryption algorithm for passwords.
options.explanation: CORS controls cross-origin response read permissions in web browsers.

questions.body: Under what circumstance does a browser send an automatic `OPTIONS` preflight request before making a cross-origin request?
questions.keyPoints: When the request is not a 'simple request' (e.g., uses methods like PUT/DELETE, custom headers like Authorization, or non-simple Content-Types).

options.text: When the request is not a 'simple request' (e.g. uses methods other than GET/POST/HEAD, has custom headers like `Authorization`, or uses `Content-Type: application/json`).
options.explanation: Browsers send an HTTP `OPTIONS` preflight request to check server permissions before issuing requests that could cause server-side mutations or leak custom headers.

options.text: Only when the user browses in Incognito / Private mode.
options.explanation: Preflight checks occur in all browser modes.

options.text: Only for WebSocket connection upgrades.
options.explanation: WebSockets use HTTP 101 Switching Protocols, not CORS OPTIONS preflights.

options.text: Whenever an image is loaded via an `` tag.
options.explanation: Standard `` tags are simple media requests that bypass CORS unless `crossorigin` attribute is set.

questions.body: What is Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) and what is its primary vector of attack?
questions.keyPoints: Attacker injects malicious client-side JavaScript into a trusted website viewed by other users.

options.text: An attack where an attacker injects malicious client-side JavaScript into a web page that executes in the browsers of victim users.
options.explanation: XSS occurs when untrusted input is rendered into the DOM without sanitization (e.g. via `innerHTML`), enabling the attacker's script to steal session tokens, cookies, or perform unauthorized actions.

options.text: An attack that overloads a web server with fake HTTP requests.
options.explanation: That describes a Denial of Service (DoS) attack.

options.text: Injecting malicious SQL syntax into backend database queries.
options.explanation: That describes SQL Injection (SQLi).

options.text: Cracking password hashes via GPU rainbow tables.
options.explanation: That describes offline password cracking.

questions.body: How does Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) work?
questions.keyPoints: Tricking an authenticated victim's browser into submitting an unauthorized request to a vulnerable site using ambient credentials (cookies).

options.text: An attacker tricks an authenticated user's browser into sending an unwanted HTTP request to a target site that automatically includes the user's stored cookies.
options.explanation: Because browsers automatically send cookies with cross-site requests by default, a malicious website can submit a form or fetch to `bank.com/transfer`, causing the server to execute the action under the victim's credentials.

options.text: An attacker reads private files off the user's local hard drive.
options.explanation: Browser sandbox prevents local file system access.

options.text: An attacker decrypts TLS traffic on a Wi-Fi router.
options.explanation: That is a Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attack.

options.text: An attacker steals source code from a GitHub repository.
options.explanation: CSRF exploits ambient browser authentication credentials.

questions.body: What is the security difference between `SameSite=Strict`, `SameSite=Lax`, and `SameSite=None` on HTTP cookies?
questions.keyPoints: Strict sends cookies only on same-site requests; Lax sends cookies on top-level safe GET navigations; None sends on all cross-site requests (requires Secure).

options.text: `Strict` sends cookies only on same-site requests; `Lax` permits cookies on top-level safe GET navigations (links); `None` sends cookies on all cross-site requests (and mandates `Secure`).
options.explanation: `SameSite=Lax` is the modern browser default, mitigating CSRF while allowing users clicking external links to arrive logged in. `Strict` provides maximal CSRF protection for sensitive sessions.

options.text: `Strict` encrypts the cookie with AES-256.
options.explanation: `SameSite` controls cross-origin transmission rules, not cookie payload encryption.

options.text: `None` deletes the cookie immediately upon receipt.
options.explanation: `None` means the cookie is sent in third-party/cross-site contexts.

options.text: `Lax` only allows cookies to be sent over HTTP, not HTTPS.
options.explanation: All SameSite settings work over HTTPS; `SameSite=None` requires HTTPS (`Secure`).

questions.body: Why should session and authentication cookies always have the `HttpOnly` and `Secure` flags set?
questions.keyPoints: HttpOnly blocks JavaScript (document.cookie) from reading the cookie, mitigating XSS; Secure ensures transmission only over HTTPS.

options.text: `HttpOnly` prevents client-side JavaScript (`document.cookie`) from reading the cookie (protecting against token theft via XSS), and `Secure` ensures the cookie is only transmitted over HTTPS.
options.explanation: Setting `HttpOnly` is a vital defense-in-depth measure against XSS token theft. `Secure` ensures sensitive authentication cookies are never transmitted over cleartext HTTP.

options.text: `HttpOnly` makes the cookie expire in 5 minutes.
options.explanation: Expiration is determined by `Max-Age` or `Expires`.

options.text: `Secure` allows cookies to be accessed across any domain without CORS.
options.explanation: `Secure` restricts transport to encrypted HTTPS connections.

options.text: `HttpOnly` disables server-side reads of the cookie.
options.explanation: The server receives and reads the cookie in HTTP request headers normally.

questions.body: What does a `Content-Security-Policy` (CSP) HTTP response header accomplish?
questions.keyPoints: Restricts the sources from which scripts, styles, images, and other resources can be loaded and executed.

options.text: It restricts which origins and domains can load scripts, styles, images, and fonts, and forbids unsafe inline scripts (`'unsafe-inline'`), mitigating XSS attacks.
options.explanation: CSP is an HTTP header (e.g. `default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' https://trusted.cdn.com`) that instructs the browser to refuse executing injected inline scripts or downloading untrusted third-party assets.

options.text: It enforces client-side password strength rules.
options.explanation: CSP governs resource loading policies, not user form validation.

options.text: It compresses HTML documents using Brotli.
options.explanation: Compression is negotiated via `Content-Encoding`.

options.text: It registers a Service Worker automatically.
options.explanation: Service Workers are registered via `navigator.serviceWorker.register()`.

questions.subtopic: HTTP Status Codes: 301 vs 302 vs 307 vs 308
questions.body: What is the critical distinction between HTTP 301/302 redirects and HTTP 307/308 redirects?
questions.keyPoints: 301/302 historically permitted changing the HTTP method (e.g. POST to GET); 307/308 strictly preserve the original request method and body.

options.text: HTTP 307 (temporary) and 308 (permanent) guarantee that the HTTP method and request body will NOT be changed (e.g. a POST stays a POST), whereas 301 and 302 historically allowed clients to rewrite POST to GET.
options.explanation: Modern specs introduced 307 and 308 to explicitly forbid user agents from changing the request method and body during redirects, fixing historical ambiguity in 301/302.

options.text: 301/302 only redirect image files.
options.explanation: Redirect codes apply to all HTTP resource requests.

options.text: 307/308 can only be used with WebSockets.
options.explanation: They are standard HTTP redirect status codes.

options.text: 308 redirects require browser restart.
options.explanation: 308 is a permanent cacheable redirect handled transparently by browsers.

questions.body: What major limitation of HTTP/1.1 does HTTP/2 solve through binary framing and multiplexing?
questions.keyPoints: Head-of-Line (HoL) blocking at the application/HTTP layer, allowing multiple requests/responses concurrently over a single TCP connection.

options.text: Application-layer Head-of-Line (HoL) blocking, by allowing hundreds of requests and responses to interleave concurrently over a single shared TCP connection.
options.explanation: In HTTP/1.1, a TCP connection can only handle one request/response at a time. HTTP/2 splits messages into binary frames multiplexed over one TCP connection, removing the need for domain sharding and sprite sheets.

options.text: Eliminating the need for TLS certificates.
options.explanation: HTTP/2 in browsers requires TLS encryption (ALPN).

options.text: Replacing IP addresses with domain hashes.
options.explanation: IP routing remains fundamental to the networking stack.

options.text: Bypassing the browser cache completely.
options.explanation: Caching mechanisms function identically over HTTP/2 and HTTP/3.

questions.body: What transport layer protocol does HTTP/3 use instead of TCP, and what problem does it eliminate?
questions.keyPoints: Uses QUIC over UDP, eliminating TCP transport-layer Head-of-Line blocking when packets are dropped.

options.text: QUIC over UDP, eliminating transport-layer Head-of-Line blocking caused by TCP packet loss (where one lost packet stalls all multiplexed streams).
options.explanation: HTTP/2 multiplexed streams over a single TCP connection, meaning one lost packet stalled the entire connection. HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP, isolating streams so packet loss in one stream does not block others.

options.text: WebSockets over TCP, eliminating HTTP headers.
options.explanation: HTTP/3 uses QUIC/UDP, not WebSockets.

options.text: Bluetooth Low Energy, eliminating Wi-Fi interference.
options.explanation: Not related to local personal area networks.

options.text: ICMP ping packets, eliminating TLS handshakes.
options.explanation: QUIC integrates TLS 1.3 encryption directly into its transport handshake.

questions.body: What happens when a browser makes a conditional request with `If-None-Match: "12345"` and the server's asset has not changed?
questions.keyPoints: Server returns HTTP 304 Not Modified with empty body, telling browser to use its cached copy.

options.text: The server responds with `HTTP 304 Not Modified` and an empty body, instructing the browser to reuse its existing cached copy.
options.explanation: ETags enable cache revalidation. If the server's current ETag matches the client's `If-None-Match`, the server returns 304 with no body, saving bandwidth and latency.

options.text: The server returns `HTTP 200 OK` and re-sends the entire asset payload.
options.explanation: Sending the full body defeats the purpose of conditional revalidation.

options.text: The browser deletes its cached file and returns an error.
options.explanation: 304 confirms the cached version is valid.

options.text: The server redirects to a CDN mirror via `HTTP 301`.
options.explanation: 304 is the dedicated cache revalidation status code.

questions.body: What is the difference between `Cache-Control: no-cache` and `Cache-Control: no-store`?
questions.keyPoints: no-cache caches the asset but forces server revalidation before reuse; no-store forbids all caching/storage entirely.

options.text: `no-cache` allows the browser to store the response in cache, but mandates revalidation with the origin server (ETag) before every reuse; `no-store` forbids storing the response anywhere in cache or disk.
options.explanation: `no-store` is for highly sensitive data (banking, private tokens) that must never touch disk caches. `no-cache` permits caching while guaranteeing freshness checks via conditional requests.

options.text: `no-store` is for mobile devices only; `no-cache` is for desktop browsers.
options.explanation: Both directives are universal HTTP/1.1 cache specifications.

options.text: `no-cache` permanently prevents the browser from saving cookies.
options.explanation: Cache-Control applies to HTTP response payload caching, not cookies.

options.text: They are exact synonyms in modern HTTP specifications.
options.explanation: Their storage and revalidation semantics are completely different.

questions.body: What does the `Strict-Transport-Security` (HSTS) response header enforce?
questions.keyPoints: Forces the browser to always connect to the website using HTTPS, automatically upgrading insecure HTTP requests.

options.text: It instructs the browser to always connect to the site using HTTPS, automatically upgrading any insecure `http://` links before sending network requests.
options.explanation: HSTS (`max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload`) prevents SSL stripping attacks by ensuring the browser never initiates an unencrypted cleartext HTTP connection to the domain.

options.text: It forces users to enter two-factor authentication tokens.
options.explanation: HSTS is a transport-layer encryption enforcement header.

options.text: It requires the client to present a client-side certificate.
options.explanation: That is Mutual TLS (mTLS), not HSTS.

options.text: It disables all cross-origin requests globally.
options.explanation: CORS and SOP govern cross-origin access, not HSTS.

questions.body:
What security protection does Subresource Integrity (SRI) provide when loading third-party scripts from a CDN:
`<script src="https://cdn.example.com/lib.js" integrity="sha384-..." crossorigin="anonymous"></script>`?
questions.keyPoints: Verifies cryptographic hash of fetched file; refuses execution if CDN has been compromised or modified.

options.text: The browser computes a cryptographic hash of the downloaded script and refuses to execute it if the hash does not match the `integrity` attribute, protecting against compromised CDNs.
options.explanation: If an attacker compromises a third-party CDN and alters `lib.js` with malicious payload, SRI fails hash validation and blocks script execution.

options.text: It accelerates CDN script download speeds through HTTP compression.
options.explanation: SRI is purely an integrity verification security feature.

options.text: It runs the third-party script in an isolated WebAssembly sandbox.
options.explanation: Valid scripts run normally in the main JavaScript context.

options.text: It automatically bypasses CORS checks.
options.explanation: SRI requires `crossorigin="anonymous"` to permit hash inspection.

questions.body: How can a web application prevent attackers from embedding its pages inside an invisible `<iframe>` to execute Clickjacking attacks?
questions.keyPoints: X-Frame-Options: DENY or SAMEORIGIN, or CSP frame-ancestors directive.

options.text: By setting the `X-Frame-Options: DENY` (or `SAMEORIGIN`) header, or using the CSP `frame-ancestors 'none'` directive.
options.explanation: Clickjacking embeds the victim site inside an opaque iframe on a malicious site. Setting `X-Frame-Options: DENY` or CSP `frame-ancestors 'none'` instructs browsers never to render the page inside iframes.

options.text: By enabling `SameSite=None` on cookies.
options.explanation: `SameSite=None` actually permits third-party cookie transmission.

options.text: By disabling JavaScript in all forms.
options.explanation: Clickjacking exploits standard mouse clicks on UI elements.

options.text: By setting `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`.
options.explanation: CORS headers do not prevent iframe embedding.

questions.body: What does the `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` header prevent?
questions.keyPoints: Prevents MIME-type sniffing where browsers execute uploaded files as scripts despite non-executable MIME types.

options.text: It prevents browsers from MIME-type sniffing (guessing content type from byte payload), enforcing that resources are strictly treated according to their declared `Content-Type`.
options.explanation: Without `nosniff`, an attacker could upload an image containing malicious script bytes; the browser might 'sniff' it as executable JavaScript, leading to XSS. `nosniff` blocks execution if MIME type is not script.

options.text: It prevents network packet sniffing by Wi-Fi packet sniffers.
options.explanation: Wi-Fi packet sniffing is mitigated by TLS encryption (HTTPS), not an HTTP response header.

options.text: It blocks search engine spiders from indexing the page.
options.explanation: That is handled by `robots.txt` or `X-Robots-Tag`.

options.text: It encrypts JSON response bodies automatically.
options.explanation: It controls browser MIME-type parsing behavior.

questions.body: Why are `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy` (COOP) and `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy` (COEP) required to use `SharedArrayBuffer` in modern browsers?
questions.keyPoints: To establish cross-origin isolation, defending against Spectre and Meltdown side-channel CPU timing attacks.

options.text: To establish a Cross-Origin Isolated browsing context, isolating the process memory to defend against hardware CPU timing attacks like Spectre.
options.explanation: High-resolution timers and `SharedArrayBuffer` can be used to construct CPU cache-timing side-channel attacks (Spectre). Browsers only enable `SharedArrayBuffer` if the site enforces process isolation via COOP and COEP.

options.text: To speed up WebGL 3D rendering framerates.
options.explanation: It is an origin-level security boundary feature, not graphics acceleration.

options.text: To bypass HTTPS certificate validation.
options.explanation: HTTPS is mandatory for cross-origin isolation.

options.text: To disable all cookies on the domain.
options.explanation: Cookies continue functioning normally.

questions.body: Why is storing sensitive JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) in browser `localStorage` considered vulnerable compared to `HttpOnly` cookies?
questions.keyPoints: Any XSS vulnerability allows malicious script to read localStorage via window.localStorage, whereas HttpOnly cookies cannot be accessed by JS.

options.text: Any Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability on the domain allows attacker scripts to directly read tokens from `localStorage`, whereas `HttpOnly` cookies cannot be accessed via JavaScript.
options.explanation: `localStorage` is fully accessible to any JavaScript running on the page. If a third-party script or XSS flaw executes, tokens stored in `localStorage` can be exfiltrated immediately.

options.text: `localStorage` is wiped automatically whenever the user closes a tab.
options.explanation: `localStorage` persists permanently on disk until cleared.

options.text: Web browsers send `localStorage` contents in plain text over the network.
options.explanation: `localStorage` is never transmitted over the network automatically.

options.text: `localStorage` cannot store strings longer than 100 characters.
options.explanation: `localStorage` has a 5-10 MB quota.

questions.body: According to the HTTP specification, what does it mean for an HTTP method to be 'Idempotent'?
questions.keyPoints: Making multiple identical requests produces the exact same side-effects on the server as making a single request.

options.text: Making multiple identical requests produces the exact same server state side-effects as making a single request (e.g. GET, PUT, DELETE).
options.explanation: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent: repeating `DELETE /user/1` or `PUT /user/1` has the same end state as executing it once. POST is typically NOT idempotent (repeating it creates duplicate records).

options.text: The request does not modify any data on the server whatsoever.
options.explanation: That is the definition of a 'Safe' method (e.g. GET, HEAD). PUT modifies data, but is idempotent.

options.text: The request is guaranteed to complete in under 100 milliseconds.
options.explanation: Latency is not part of HTTP method idempotency definitions.

options.text: The response cannot be cached by intermediate proxies.
options.explanation: Caching rules are determined by headers, not idempotency.

questions.body: What HTTP status code and header does a server return when successfully accepting a WebSocket upgrade request?
questions.keyPoints: HTTP 101 Switching Protocols with Upgrade: websocket and Connection: Upgrade headers.

options.text: `HTTP 101 Switching Protocols` with `Upgrade: websocket` and `Connection: Upgrade` headers.
options.explanation: WebSocket connections initiate as standard HTTP/1.1 requests requesting an upgrade. The server responds with `101 Switching Protocols`, transitioning the TCP socket into full-duplex WebSocket framing.

options.text: `HTTP 200 OK` with `Content-Type: application/websocket`.
options.explanation: Status 200 is standard response, not a protocol switch.

options.text: `HTTP 204 No Content`.
options.explanation: 204 is for completed actions with no return body.

options.text: `HTTP 307 Temporary Redirect` to `ws://`.
options.explanation: The handshake upgrades the existing TCP socket in place via code 101.
